title: Relative pronouns
subtitle: the man (that) I met / Professor Johnson, whom I admire
summary: Choose between who, whom, which, that and no relative pronoun in defining and non-defining relative clauses.

lesson.heading: When can the pronoun be left out?
lesson.text: A relative pronoun that is the object of its clause can be left out. One that is the subject of its clause cannot, because the clause would then have no subject.

examples.text: We went to a beach **(which / that)** Ali had recommended to us.
examples.note: the subject of the clause is Ali, so the pronoun can go

examples.text: I know a man **who / that** ran in the New York Marathon last year.
examples.note: the pronoun is the subject, so it has to stay

lesson.heading: Defining relative clauses
rows: which, that, or no relative pronoun
who, whom, that, or no relative pronoun
lesson.note: A defining clause tells us which person or thing we mean, and takes no commas.

lesson.heading: Formal or informal?
lesson.text: As object, that or no relative pronoun sounds natural in conversation; which is the formal choice for things, and whom is very formal and rare in speech.

examples.note: rather than ... which ... in this informal context

examples.text: He's the man **(that)** I met at Aisha's party.
examples.note: rather than ... who / whom I met ...

examples.text: The boy **whom** Elena had shouted at smiled.
examples.note: less formally: that, no relative pronoun, or who

lesson.heading: that after something, all, much, superlatives
lesson.text: We use that as subject after something and anything; after all, little, much and none used as pronouns; and after noun phrases that include a superlative. which is also possible after something and anything, but is less common.

examples.text: These walls are all **that** remain of the city.
examples.wrong: all which remain of the city

examples.text: There was little **that** we could do to help her.
She's one of the kindest people **(that)** I know.
examples.wrong: one of the kindest people who I know

lesson.note: As object after these words, that or no relative pronoun is used: There's something (that) I should tell you.

lesson.heading: Non-defining relative clauses
lesson.note: A non-defining clause adds extra information and is marked off by commas. The relative pronoun can never be left out.

lesson.heading: Non-defining clauses in use
lesson.text: In a non-defining clause we must include a relative pronoun. who or whom can be the object, though whom is very formal; which works as subject or object for things.

examples.text: Professor Johnson, **who(m)** I have long admired, is to visit the university next week.
The Master's course, **which** I took in 2001, is no longer taught.
examples.note: or ... that I took ..., which some people think is incorrect

examples.text: He received a low mark for his essay, **which** was only one page long.

lesson.text: Look for a comma: after a comma the pronoun always stays, and that becomes questionable.

exercises.prompt: He pointed to the stairs ___ led down to the cellar.
exercises.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of a defining clause about things, so which or that - and it can't be left out.

exercises.prompt: She was greatly influenced by her father, ___ she adored.
exercises.explanation: A non-defining clause about a person always keeps its pronoun; whom is the formal option.

exercises.prompt: These walls are all ___ remain of the city.
exercises.explanation: After all used as a pronoun we use that as subject, not which.

exercises.prompt: She's one of the kindest people ___ I know.
exercises.explanation: After a noun phrase with a superlative we use that or no relative pronoun.

exercises.prompt: Can the relative pronoun in bold be left out?

items.text: We talked about the party **which** Natalia wants to organise for my birthday.
To get to Maxim's house, take the main road **that** bypasses the village.
Let's go through the main points **that** he made in his lecture.
He received a low mark for his essay, **which** was only one page long.
Dev is a friend **who** we stayed with in Australia.
The couple **who** live next to us have 16 grandchildren.
There was little **that** we could do to help her.
Mrs Yang, **who** is 42, has three children.

exercises.statement: Yesterday was the hottest day I can remember.
exercises.explanation: Correct. The pronoun is the object after a superlative noun phrase, so it can be left out (... the hottest day that I can remember is also fine).

exercises.statement: There isn't much can go wrong with the machine.
exercises.explanation: There isn't much that can go wrong with the machine. After much used as a pronoun, that is the subject of the clause and can't be dropped.

exercises.statement: Thieves whom stole paintings from Notford art gallery have been arrested in Paris.
exercises.explanation: Thieves who stole paintings from Notford art gallery have been arrested in Paris. whom is only used as an object, never as the subject.

exercises.statement: The boy took the photograph was paid £100.
exercises.explanation: The boy who took the photograph was paid £100. A subject relative pronoun can't be left out.

exercises.prompt: It may be the most important decision ___ you will ever take.
exercises.explanation: After a noun phrase containing a superlative we prefer that (or no relative pronoun) to which.

exercises.prompt: The problems faced by the company, ___ I'll look at in detail in a moment, are being resolved.
exercises.explanation: This is a non-defining clause about things, so which - and the pronoun is obligatory.

exercises.prompt: Add the information 'he is over 80' to 'Eva's father has just come back from a skiing holiday' as a non-defining relative clause.
exercises.answer: Eva's father, who is over 80, has just come back from a skiing holiday.
exercises.explanation: The extra information goes between commas immediately after the noun it describes.
